pumac-2021-power-01.title: A line through the origin
pumac-2021-power-01.body:
Take $W=\{(t,0):t\in\mathbb R\}$, the $x$-axis. It is non-trivial ($(1,0)\in W$) and not all of $\mathbb R^2$ ($(0,1)\notin W$).

It contains $0=(0,0)$, and for $(s,0),(t,0)\in W$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ we get $(s,0)+(t,0)=(s+t,0)\in W$ and $\lambda(t,0)=(\lambda t,0)\in W$. The vector space axioms (commutativity, associativity, distributivity, ...) hold in $W$ because they hold in $\mathbb R^2$. So $W$ is a subspace. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-02.title: Rescale the standard basis
pumac-2021-power-02.body:
The form is diagonal in the standard basis, so the standard basis vectors are already orthogonal: $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=0$ for $i\neq j$. Only the lengths need fixing, since $\langle e_1,e_1\rangle=1$, $\langle e_2,e_2\rangle=2$, $\langle e_3,e_3\rangle=3$.

Divide each vector by its length:
$$u_1=e_1=(1,0,0),\quad u_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}e_2=\left(0,\tfrac1{\sqrt2},0\right),\quad u_3=\tfrac1{\sqrt3}e_3=\left(0,0,\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\right).$$
Check: $\langle u_2,u_2\rangle=2\cdot\frac12=1$, $\langle u_3,u_3\rangle=3\cdot\frac13=1$, and all mixed products vanish. Three mutually orthogonal unit vectors are linearly independent, so they form a basis. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-03.title: Injective linear map between spaces of equal dimension
pumac-2021-power-03.body:
Define $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ by $T(w)=(\langle v_1,w\rangle,\dots,\langle v_n,w\rangle)$. It is linear because the inner product is linear in each argument.

**Injective.** If $T(w)=0$ then $\langle v_i,w\rangle=0$ for all $i$. Since the $v_i$ span $\mathbb R^n$, write $w=\sum c_iv_i$; then $\langle w,w\rangle=\sum c_i\langle v_i,w\rangle=0$, so $w=0$ by positive-definiteness. Hence $\ker T=\{0\}$.

By $\dim\mathbb R^n=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T$ we get $\dim\operatorname{im}T=n$, so $T$ is surjective. Thus for every $(\alpha_i)$ there is a $w$ with $T(w)=(\alpha_i)$, and it is unique since $T$ is injective. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-04.title: Eigenbasis expansion
pumac-2021-power-04.body:
Let $u_1,\dots,u_n$ be an orthonormal eigenbasis, $Au_i=\lambda_iu_i$, with $\lambda=\max\lambda_i$. For $x=\sum c_iu_i\neq0$ we have $Ax=\sum c_i\lambda_iu_i$, so by orthonormality
$$\langle x,Ax\rangle=\sum_i\lambda_ic_i^2\le\lambda\sum_ic_i^2=\lambda\langle x,x\rangle.$$
Hence the quotient is at most $\lambda$ for every $x\ne0$.

If $\lambda=\lambda_j$, then $x=u_j$ gives $\frac{\langle u_j,Au_j\rangle}{\langle u_j,u_j\rangle}=\lambda_j=\lambda$. So the supremum is attained and equals $\lambda$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-05.title: Discriminant argument
pumac-2021-power-05.body:
Let $B(x,y)=\langle x,Ay\rangle$. It is bilinear, symmetric (because $A$ is self-adjoint: $B(x,y)=\langle x,Ay\rangle=\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle y,Ax\rangle=B(y,x)$) and $B(z,z)\ge0$ for all $z$.

For $t\in\mathbb R$:
$$0\le B(x+ty,x+ty)=B(x,x)+2tB(x,y)+t^2B(y,y).$$
*Case $B(y,y)>0$.* A quadratic in $t$ that is never negative has non-positive discriminant: $4B(x,y)^2-4B(x,x)B(y,y)\le0$, which is the claim.

*Case $B(y,y)=0$.* Then $0\le B(x,x)+2tB(x,y)$ for all real $t$, which forces $B(x,y)=0$ (otherwise let $t\to\pm\infty$ with the sign making $2tB(x,y)$ very negative). The claim reads $0\le0$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-06.title: Reduce to an eigenvector equation
pumac-2021-power-06.body:
Let $P=[p_{ij}]$; all entries are positive. The probability of being on pad $k$ after one step, starting from distribution $\pi$, is $\sum_j\pi_jp_{jk}=(P^T\pi)_k$. So $\pi$ works at all times if and only if $P^T\pi=\pi$ (if this holds once it holds forever; conversely time $1$ gives it).

**The top eigenvalue is 1.** Rows of $P$ sum to $1$, so $P\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1$ and $1$ is an eigenvalue of $P$. Let $\lambda$ be the top eigenvalue of $P$. By (c) there is $v$ with all entries $>0$ and $P^Tv=\lambda v$. Summing the entries: $\sum_k(P^Tv)_k=\sum_jv_j\sum_kp_{jk}=\sum_jv_j$, while this also equals $\lambda\sum_jv_j$. As $\sum v_j>0$, $\lambda=1$.

**Existence.** Normalise $v$ so its entries sum to $1$: $\pi=v/\sum v_j$ is a probability vector with $P^T\pi=\pi$.

**Uniqueness.** $P^T$ has all entries positive and the same characteristic polynomial as $P$, hence the same eigenvalues, so its top eigenvalue is also $1$. By (b) applied to $P^T$, the $1$-eigenspace of $P^T$ is one-dimensional. Any stationary distribution lies in it and has coordinate sum $1$, so it equals $\pi$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-07.title: All transpositions are conjugate
pumac-2021-power-07.body:
Let $\chi$ be a character. From $\chi(\mathrm{id})=\chi(\mathrm{id})^2$ and $\chi=\pm1$ we get $\chi(\mathrm{id})=1$, hence $\chi(\sigma^{-1})=\chi(\sigma)^{-1}=\chi(\sigma)$.

For a transposition $\tau=(a\,b)$ and any $\sigma\in S_n$, $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma(a)\,\sigma(b))$ is again a transposition, and every transposition arises this way. Also $\chi(\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1})=\chi(\sigma)\chi(\tau)\chi(\sigma)=\chi(\tau)$. So $\chi$ takes the same value $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$ on all transpositions.

Every permutation is a product of transpositions, so $\chi(\pi)=\varepsilon^{k}$ for any such product of $k$ transpositions. Thus $\chi$ is determined by $\varepsilon$, and there are **at most two** characters.

**Existence of two.** $\varepsilon=1$ gives the trivial character. For $\varepsilon=-1$, let $P_\pi$ be the linear map with $P_\pi e_i=e_{\pi(i)}$ and set $\chi(\pi)=\det P_\pi=D(e_{\pi(1)},\dots,e_{\pi(n)})$. Swapping two arguments of $D$ multiplies it by $-1$, so reordering $e_{\pi(1)},\dots,e_{\pi(n)}$ into $e_1,\dots,e_n$ by swaps shows $\det P_\pi=\pm1$. Since $P_{\pi_1\circ\pi_2}=P_{\pi_1}P_{\pi_2}$, multiplicativity of $\det$ shows $\chi$ is a character; for a transposition $P_\tau$ is one swap, so $\chi(\tau)=-1$. So there are **exactly two** characters. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-08.title: Dependent rows
pumac-2021-power-08.body:
Row $2-$ row $1=(3,3,3)=$ row $3-$ row $2$, so $R_1-2R_2+R_3=0$ and the rows are linearly dependent; hence the determinant is $0$.

Direct expansion: $1(45-48)-2(36-42)+3(32-35)=-3+12-9=0$.

**Answer: 0**

pumac-2021-power-09.title: Repeated arguments give zero
pumac-2021-power-09.body:
If two arguments are equal, swapping them leaves the input unchanged but multiplies $D$ by $-1$, so $D=-D$ and $D=0$.

Since the vectors are dependent, some $v_j=\sum_{i\ne j}a_iv_i$. By multilinearity in the $j$th slot,
$$D(\dots,v_j,\dots)=\sum_{i\neq j}a_iD(\dots,v_i,\dots,)$$
where in each term $v_i$ appears twice (in slot $i$ and slot $j$), so every term is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

pumac-2021-power-10.title: Use $A^TA=I$
pumac-2021-power-10.body:
Let $A$ be the matrix whose columns are $v_1,\dots,v_n$, so $D(v_1,\dots,v_n)=\det A$. Then $(A^TA)_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$, i.e. $A^TA=I$.

From the permutation formula, $\det A^T=\sum_\pi\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_ia_{\pi(i)\,i}=\sum_\pi\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_ja_{j\,\pi^{-1}(j)}=\det A$, using $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ and re-indexing by $\pi^{-1}$.

Therefore $(\det A)^2=\det(A^T)\det A=\det(A^TA)=\det I=1$, so $|\det A|=1$.

**Answer: 1**

pumac-2021-power-11.title: Verify the axioms
pumac-2021-power-11.body:
*Non-negativity and definiteness:* each term $|x_k-y_k|\ge0$, so $d_{TV}\ge0$, and the sum is $0$ iff $x_k=y_k$ for all $k$, i.e. $x=y$.

*Symmetry:* $|x_k-y_k|=|y_k-x_k|$.

*Triangle inequality:* for $x,y,z\in\Delta_d$ and each $k$, $|x_k-z_k|\le|x_k-y_k|+|y_k-z_k|$. Summing over $k$ and multiplying by $\frac12$ gives $d_{TV}(x,z)\le d_{TV}(x,y)+d_{TV}(y,z)$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-12.title: Split by quadrant
pumac-2021-power-12.body:
Take $x=0$. The ball is $\{y:|y_1|+|y_2|<r\}$. In the first quadrant this is $y_1+y_2<r$, a triangle with vertices $(0,0),(r,0),(0,r)$ (without the hypotenuse); the other quadrants are its reflections.

Together they form the open square (diamond) with vertices $(\pm r,0),(0,\pm r)$, whose sides have slope $\pm1$ and side length $r\sqrt2$, boundary excluded. For a general centre $x$, translate by $x$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-power-13.title: Symmetry of the cube
pumac-2021-power-13.body:
For a permutation $\sigma$ of $[n]$ let $R_\sigma=\{x\in[0,1]^n:x_{\sigma(1)}\le\dots\le x_{\sigma(n)}\}$. These $n!$ regions cover the cube $[0,1]^n$ (sort the coordinates of any point) and two of them overlap only inside a hyperplane $\{x_i=x_j\}$, which has volume $0$. Each $R_\sigma$ is the image of the simplex under a coordinate permutation, which preserves volume. Hence $n!\cdot\mathrm{Vol}=\mathrm{Vol}([0,1]^n)=1$.

**Answer: $\frac1{n!}$**

pumac-2021-power-14.title: One orthant, then multiply
pumac-2021-power-14.body:
The ball is symmetric under each sign change $x_i\to-x_i$, so its volume is $2^n$ times the volume of the part with all $x_i\ge0$: the simplex $S=\{x_i\ge0,\ \sum x_i\le1\}$.

The linear map $y_k=x_1+\dots+x_k$ has a triangular matrix with $1$s on the diagonal, so determinant $1$ and it preserves volume. It maps $S$ onto $\{0\le y_1\le y_2\le\dots\le y_n\le1\}$, whose volume is $\frac1{n!}$ by part (a). So $\mathrm{Vol}(S)=\frac1{n!}$ and the ball has volume $\frac{2^n}{n!}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2^n}{n!}$**

pumac-2021-power-15.title: Reduce to an orthogonal box
pumac-2021-power-15.body:
**Dependent case.** If the $v_i$ are dependent, $Z(B)$ lies in a proper subspace, so has volume $0$, and $D=0$ by Problem 1.14(b).

**Independent case.** Two operations:
- *Scaling* $v_i\to\lambda v_i$: $D$ gets multiplied by $\lambda$ (multilinearity); $Z$ is stretched by $|\lambda|$ in one direction, so its volume is multiplied by $|\lambda|$.
- *Shear* $v_i\to v_i+cv_j$ ($j\ne i$): $D$ is unchanged (the extra term has $v_j$ twice). $Z$ changes by a shear along direction $v_j$: slicing by lines parallel to $v_j$ (Cavalieri), each slice is a segment of the same length translated, so the volume is unchanged.

Run Gram–Schmidt on $v_1,\dots,v_n$: $w_1=v_1$, $w_i=v_i-\sum_{j<i}c_{ij}w_j$. Each step is a shear (as each $w_j$ is a combination of $v_1..v_j$, adding multiples of earlier vectors, apply shears in order), so $D(w)=D(v)$ and $\mathrm{Vol}Z(w)=\mathrm{Vol}Z(v)$. The $w_i$ are mutually orthogonal and nonzero, and $Z(w)$ is a box with side lengths $\|w_i\|$: its volume is $\prod\|w_i\|$ (a rigid motion maps it to an axis-parallel box).

On the other hand $w_i/\|w_i\|$ is an orthonormal basis, so by Problem 1.14(c) and scaling, $|D(w_1,\dots,w_n)|=\prod\|w_i\|\cdot|D(\hat w_1,\dots,\hat w_n)|=\prod\|w_i\|$. Hence $\mathrm{Vol}Z(v)=\mathrm{Vol}Z(w)=|D(w)|=|D(v)|$. $\blacksquare$
